terms.grammar: the passive of invehō, with in and the accusative
evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 2.3.3: vehementer est in Pompejum invectus
Cic. Fam. 12.25.4: sīc sum in Antōnium invectus
Cic. Fam. 5.2.6: nōn oportuisse Metellum … oppugnārī ā mē (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fin. 2.80: aliquem maledictīs īnsectārī (Lewis & Short)
Sall. J. 29.2: ā prīncipiō ācerrimē rēgem impugnāverat (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 148, 274: competītōrēs suōs inpugnat, he attacks his opponents

phrases.latin: eō diē Catō vehementer est in Pompejum invectus et eum ōrātiōne perpetuā tamquam reum accūsāvit
phrases.english: that day Cato attacked Pompey fiercely and accused him in a long speech as though he were on trial

phrases.latin: sīc sum in Antōnium invectus ut ille nōn ferret
phrases.english: I attacked Antony so hard that he could not bear it

sources: Lewis & Short: inveho · Lewis & Short: oppugno · Lewis & Short: insector · Lewis & Short: impugno
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 148, 274.
Cicero’s letters to Quintus and to his friends (Purser), checked against the Perseus Latin texts and the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (9 November 2026).
Citations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them and have not been checked against an edition.
